In her Bengaluru hostel room, Keerthana lay awake again, replaying the last call with Ammamma. It had been four months.
"Come for Pongal, kanna," Ammamma had said. "I'll make your sweet pongal."
"Next month, promise. Exams."
Next month never came.
If only she had taken the bus that weekend. If only she'd noticed that Ammamma's voice sounded tired. If only, if only. Every night the call played, and every night she changed her answer.
Siddharth, her friend from the next wing, found her on the steps one morning. "Keerthu, you couldn't have known. The doctors didn't know."
"But if I'd gone..."
"It still wouldn't have been in your hands." She stared at her shoes and didn't answer.

qa.q: What did Ammamma say she would make for Keerthana?
qa.a: Sweet pongal.

qa.q: What is Keerthana feeling as she replays the call each night?
qa.a: She feels guilty and grieving, imagining that a different answer could have changed what happened.

qa.q: What turning point could help Keerthana out of the loop?
qa.a: Hearing, perhaps from a counsellor as well as Siddharth, that the death was never in her hands, and grieving without the what-ifs.

qa.q: What is Siddharth experiencing as he tries to reassure her?
qa.a: He seems concerned and a little helpless, wanting to lift her guilt but seeing she can't accept it yet.

grounding: Shows a young woman replaying her grandmother's last call and blaming herself for not visiting sooner, a guilt that loops for months.

It's been six months since Dida died, and I still replay that call. She rang on a Wednesday. I was in the library. I whispered, "Dida, I'll call you on Sunday." She said, "Okay, shona, eat well."
She died on Friday.
Looking back, I've built a hundred other Wednesdays. In one, I take the train home. In another, I hear her cough and phone the doctor. In every one, I save her. My sister Kashish says, "Arnab, she was eighty-seven. Her heart was tired." I know that. But the what-ifs feel better than helplessness, somehow. At least in them I could have done something.
I think I'll talk to the college counsellor next week. The loop is getting old.

qa.a: She died on Friday.

qa.q: Why do the what-ifs feel better to Arnab than helplessness?
qa.a: Arnab's guilt gives a feeling of control, as if the death could have been stopped, which hurts less than feeling powerless.

Karthik had five minutes before his seminar presentation, the professor already tapping the projector, when someone behind him opened a tiffin. Rasam. Pepper and tamarind, exactly like Amma's.
It had been eight months. He'd been fine for weeks. Fine at Diwali, even.
Now his throat closed and his eyes filled, right there in the second row. He pressed his thumb hard into his palm.
Thomas, beside him, glanced over. "You okay?"
"It's stupid. It's the smell."
"Not stupid." Thomas passed him a tissue without making a show of it. "Want me to go first?"
Karthik nodded. He wasn't going backwards, he told himself. It was just a wave.

The Hyderabad office had strung up Diwali lights over the weekend. Mahima walked in on Monday, saw the rows of little diyas at reception, and had to go straight to the washroom.
Last Diwali, Papa had lit every one of them on their balcony, humming off-key.

"Reena? Reena, what's wrong?"
"Nothing. It's this song, Noor."
The café speaker was playing an old film melody. Reena's cheeks were wet.
"Your Nana's song?"
"He sang it every morning while shaving. Badly." She laughed and cried at once. "It's been nearly a year. I was fine. Why now?"
"Because you loved him."
"I feel like I'm back at the start."
"You're not. You've had good days. This is just a wave."
"A wave?"
"That's what my aunt calls it. It comes, and then it goes."
Reena wiped her face and held her cup with both hands until the song ended.

Kishore marked 14 March on the calendar in his Pune flat in red. One year since Appa.
He'd learned from the last few months: Appa's birthday had flattened him without warning, and he had spent it alone. This time he made a plan.
He called Parveen. "Will you come with me that morning? Just to the temple, then breakfast."
"Of course."
On the day, at the temple steps, Kishore's eyes filled. He didn't fight it. "This is just grief," he said quietly, the way the counsellor had suggested. Parveen stood beside him.
Afterwards, they ate idlis at Appa's favourite place. The tears came again, briefly, and passed. Kishore ordered a second coffee.

Looking back at my first year without Nani, I learned something about hard dates. The first Holi came without warning and knocked me flat. I stayed in bed all day and felt stupid for it.
So for her death anniversary, I planned. I asked Parveen to come over. We made Nani's gulab jamuns, which came out lumpy. I lit a diya by her photo.

I'm Mahima, and now every hard date gets a plan and a friend.

Diary, two weeks after
Amma died on the 3rd. Two years of hospital visits, night feeds, oxygen cylinders. Two years of me sleeping on the floor beside her bed.
And the thing I can't tell anyone: the first morning after, I slept until nine. I woke up and there was no alarm, no medicine chart, and for one second I felt light. Relieved.
Then I felt sick. What kind of daughter feels relieved?
Deepika came over today. I almost told her. I said, "I miss her so much," which is true. I didn't say the other thing, which is also true.
Maybe next time.
Leela

In the small town of Mapusa, the house was quiet again after the funeral crowds left. Shalini sat on the verandah where she'd pushed Avó's wheelchair every evening for four years.
Francis from next door came with a pot of tea, as he had every day of the illness.
"How are you really?" he asked.
Shalini looked at the empty wheelchair. "Honestly? I slept a full night for the first time in four years. And I felt... lighter. And now I feel terrible for feeling lighter."
Francis nodded slowly. "My mother said the same after my father. It doesn't mean you didn't love her."
Shalini's shoulders dropped. She reached for the tea and cried, properly, for the first time.

Dear Vidya,
Today is four years since Ma died. I made her lemon rice this morning, the way she taught me, with too many curry leaves. It still doesn't taste exactly like hers.
You asked me last year whether it gets easier. It changes. For the first two years I couldn't even open her recipe notebook. I went to a counsellor for a while, because everything felt stuck. That helped more than I expected.
Now I laugh at her notes in the margins: "Pankaj, don't burn it." I still miss her. But I also live. I got the job, I moved cities, and I think she'd be proud.
Come over on Sunday? I'll make the lemon rice.
Pankaj

People ask me what you do when a friend loses a parent. I'm Joseph, and I got it wrong for a while.
When Samir's mother died in January, I was there for the funeral. Then, like everyone, I went back to normal. I didn't mention her. I thought I was being kind.
In April, Samir said, "Everyone's forgotten her." That hit me.
So I changed. I started saying her name. "Your Ammi would've hated this movie." Every few weeks I'd text, "Walk tonight?" or bring biryani over. I'd ask, "How are you today?" not "How are you?"
It's not a big gesture. It's just showing up again and again. And he talks about her now. Laughs about her, even.

Pallavi beti, you think you need more coffee to study? Let me tell you about me in Class 12.
I was the topper in our town. I wanted to stay the topper. So I drank tea after tea, strong, and studied till three in the morning. I caught every cold going round. I stopped playing the harmonium, which I loved. My friends called, and I said I was busy.
When I felt tired, I thought, Ramesh, you're getting lazy. So I pushed harder.
One day I fell asleep on my bicycle, beta. Right into a ditch. Only then did my father sit me down and make me rest.
Tired is not lazy, Pallavi. Your old uncle learned it the hard way.

Karthik, you're rolling your eyes at your project. I know that look. Let me tell you something from my final year of engineering.
I was a girl of twenty-one then. By the last semester, I was so tired that everything seemed pointless. Projects? Pointless. Placements? A lottery. When my friend Radha stayed up to perfect her circuit, I said, "Why bother? Nobody reads these." I laughed at people who still cared. I thought I was being clever.
Later I understood. I wasn't clever. I was exhausted. Caring had become too expensive, so I stopped.
My professor noticed. She asked me, "Neelam, when did you last sleep properly?" That question cracked something open. So, Karthik, when you sneer, ask yourself that.

qa.q: What was Neelam's friend Radha doing?
qa.a: Staying up to perfect her circuit.

qa.q: What was young Neelam feeling when she laughed at people who cared?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and detached, protecting herself because caring had become too expensive.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point helped Neelam?
qa.a: Her professor asking when she last slept properly, which helped her see the cynicism was exhaustion.

qa.q: How might Radha have felt when Neelam said "Why bother?"
qa.a: Radha may have felt hurt and discouraged by her friend's sneer at work she cared about.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling her final-year cynicism, sneering at friends who cared, as an exhausted mind's protection.

Chinmay was at the next bench, rewiring his drone for the fifth time. "Lalit, can you check my code?"

Supervisor's note, Friday
Preeti joined the lab in June and was quick and careful. Over the last three weeks I've seen a change. Simple data entry that used to take her an hour now takes most of the morning. She mislabelled two sample sets this week, which she has never done before. Today I found her staring at the same spreadsheet for twenty minutes.
When I asked if she was okay, she said, "I don't know why I'm even here. I'm a fraud." She has been working late every night.
I told her the mistakes are fixable and she is not a fraud. I have reduced her tasks for next week and asked her to see the student counsellor. I'll check in on Monday.
Damini

qa.q: How many sample sets did Preeti mislabel this week?

qa.q: What might Damini have felt on finding Preeti staring at the same spreadsheet?
qa.a: Damini was likely concerned and worried, noticing a once quick, careful intern suddenly struggling and working late.

qa.a: Effort alone won't fix exhaustion; reducing tasks and involving the counsellor gives her room to recover.

qa.q: How might Preeti experience Damini's response?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and less alone, hearing she is not a fraud and that her load is lighter.

grounding: Shows a supervisor's note on a student whose simple tasks take longer and mistakes multiply, feeling like a fraud, and support offered.
